rv.q: But somehow life and joy trickles into this room all the same – the curtains can’t shut everything out. Kristin Scott Thomas plays lady of the house Ranevskaya with a compelling kind of apathy.
This lively, irreverent version brings tremendous immediacy to the piece.

Kristin Scott Thomas is back at the Harold Pinter theatre, banishing memories of 2023’s misfiring MeToo comedy drama Lyonesse by tackling, supremely well, Chekhov’s elegiac last masterpiece, The Cherry Orchard.
But some of the edges are softened, such as the fire of student and would-be revolutionary Trofimov (Jack Riddiford).
But it’s a production that refuses to pin itself down.
Otherwise, it's like watching a herd of cats purposelessly gathered on Chloe Lamford's damp-riddled set.
This performance is bound to be a night of heartwarming, witty theatre.
Rickson’s direction is masterful, alive to every nuance, confidently embracing the dualities in Chekhov’s text.
The production continues at Harold Pinter until 9th January and runs 2 hours 30 mins including interval.
But Ian Rickson’s production doesn’t quite catch all the heights and depths of the emotions, the technical efficiency rather limiting the stakes.
Rickson and McPherson's revival of The Cherry Orchard is a beautiful rendition of a timeless play.
As this bunch of nervous aristos raise a glass or five at what could be their final knees-up, it all hangs off of Scott Thomas, who feels birthed to deliver Chekhov's profundities.
This feeling of a whole community affected by a progress they don't want but perhaps need is the tenure of McPherson's adaptation where emotional suffering is just something you have to do.
All in all, this is a fun and touching restaging of a classic family drama.
McPherson’s adaptation is expletive-laden and very frank, highlighting the hypocrisy of a family who cannot articulate their feelings or act in a way that serves their interest.
As such, Rickson and McPherson’s The Cherry Orchard is far more entertaining than it is intellectual and emotive, meaning it ought to have been a lot more fruitful.
The result is a confused and incohesive production that feels at odds with the intent of Chekhov’s original.
Although the humour is perfectly balanced in this solid production, the emotional connection to its lead characters are somewhat sacrificed.

cn.t: McPherson's accessible adaptation and Rickson's solid direction deliver a respectable but unspectacular Cherry Orchard, with Kristin Scott Thomas praised for her modern, hard-edged Ranevskaya in a production that leans heavily into comedy.
